organism: Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus) serogroup B, defined by its polysaccharide capsule structure like the other 11 known serogroups. Unlike serogroups A, C, W, and Y, the serogroup B capsular polysaccharide closely resembles a human neural cell adhesion molecule and is poorly immunogenic and potentially unsafe as a vaccine antigen - which is why serogroup B vaccines use different, protein-based antigens (factor H binding protein and others) rather than a polysaccharide conjugate approach. See the companion Meningococcal (A, C, W, Y) chapter for organism biology, pathogenesis, and general epidemiology shared across all serogroups.
clinicalFeaturesSummary: Clinical presentation is not distinguishable by serogroup: meningitis (about 50% of US invasive cases), meningococcal septicemia (about 30%, with petechial/purpuric rash, shock, and multiorgan failure risk), and bacteremic pneumonia (about 15%) all occur regardless of which serogroup is responsible. Case-fatality overall is 10%-15% even with treatment, with up to 20% of survivors left with permanent sequelae such as hearing loss or neurologic damage.
epidemiologySummary: Serogroup B is disproportionately a disease of young people in the US: it causes about 60% of invasive meningococcal disease in children and young adults under 24, versus a much smaller share in older adults, where serogroups C, W, and Y predominate instead. College students specifically face more than 3 times the serogroup B risk of similarly aged people not attending college. Serogroup B outbreaks among university students were a recurring feature of 2010-2018 US surveillance data, alongside serogroup C outbreaks in other populations.
secularTrendsSummary: Serogroup B is one of the two leading causes of meningococcal disease in the US, responsible for roughly 25%-40% of the 329 total cases reported nationally in 2018 (0.10 per 100,000 population) - a share that has stayed relatively stable even as overall incidence has declined from a late-1990s peak. Because serogroup B disproportionately affects people under 24, and because routine MenACWY vaccination doesn't touch serogroup B at all, this age group's meningococcal risk profile looks meaningfully different from older adults'.
vaccineDescription: Two recombinant serogroup B vaccines are licensed in the US, both approved for ages 10-25: MenB-FHbp (Trumenba) and MenB-4C (Bexsero). Both are given intramuscularly and contain aluminum adjuvant; Bexsero additionally contains kanamycin as an antibiotic, and its prefilled syringe tip caps contain latex. Trumenba and Bexsero are NOT interchangeable - the same brand must be used for every dose in a series, including boosters.
vaccinationScheduleSummary: For people at increased risk (see Special Risk Groups), ACIP recommends either a 2-dose Bexsero series (0 and 1 month or longer) or a 3-dose Trumenba series (0, 1-2, and 6 months). For healthy adolescents 16-23 without an elevated-risk condition, MenB vaccination is offered via shared clinical decision-making for short-term protection, preferably at 16-18, using either a 2-dose Bexsero series (0 and 1 month+) or a 2-dose Trumenba series (0 and 6 months) - note this is a different dosing pattern for Trumenba than the 3-dose high-risk schedule. If a Bexsero second dose is given earlier than the minimum interval, it must be repeated at least 4 weeks after the last dose; if a Trumenba second dose is given at 6+ months, no third dose is needed, but if a third dose is given too early it must be repeated at least 4 months after the prior dose. MenB vaccine may be given simultaneously or at any interval relative to other live or inactivated vaccines, including MenACWY.
vaccineEfficacySummary: Efficacy is assessed via serum bactericidal antibody response against a panel of representative serogroup B strains (since serogroup B strains are more antigenically diverse than A/C/W/Y, a single correlate doesn't capture protection as cleanly). In a US trial, 81%-84% of adolescents achieved a composite bactericidal response after the Trumenba series. In a UK trial of college students, 88% of Bexsero recipients had a composite response at 1 month post-series, but that fell to 66% by 11 months - and only 63% of adolescents in a separate Australia/Canada trial achieved a composite response - underscoring that MenB protection, like MenACWY protection, should not be assumed to be durable or uniform across studies.
contraindicationsSummary: For both Trumenba and Bexsero, a severe allergic reaction after a previous dose or to any vaccine component is a contraindication. Latex sensitivity is a precaution specific to Bexsero, since its prefilled syringe tip caps contain natural rubber latex. Moderate or severe acute illness is a general precaution. No randomized trials have evaluated MenB vaccination in pregnancy; ACIP recommends deferring Bexsero or Trumenba in pregnant women unless the individual is at increased risk and, after discussion with her provider, the benefits are judged to outweigh the potential risks.
vaccineSafetySummary: Trumenba: local injection-site pain in 72%-93% of recipients, with induration and erythema also common; systemic reactions include headache (27%-67%), fatigue (30%-66%), myalgia, and arthralgia, mostly resolving within 5 days. VAERS review (2014-2018) found only expected adverse events, no new safety signal, including during a real-world mass vaccination campaign on a university campus. Bexsero: even more frequent local reactions (pain in 82%-98%, erythema 35%-68%, swelling 26%-47%), plus headache, fatigue, myalgia, and arthralgia systemically. VAERS review (2015-2018) similarly found no new safety signal, though transient decreased arm mobility at the injection site was disproportionately reported, and a US mass-vaccination evaluation found 0.88 syncopal events per 1,000 doses.
vaccineStorageSummary: Both Bexsero and Trumenba must be stored at refrigerator temperature, 2C to 8C (36F to 46F). See CDC's Vaccine Storage and Handling Toolkit for complete guidance.
surveillanceSummary: Meningococcal disease of any serogroup is reportable in all US states; serogroup confirmation (via slide agglutination or real-time PCR after a positive culture or PCR from a sterile site) is what specifically distinguishes serogroup B cases for surveillance purposes, since presentation alone can't do it. See CDC's Manual for the Surveillance of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases for reporting guidance.

supplementalTopics.title: Special Risk Groups Recommended for Vaccination
supplementalTopics.summary: ACIP recommends MenB vaccine, starting at age 10, for people with persistent complement component deficiencies (including eculizumab or ravulizumab use), functional or anatomic asplenia (including sickle cell disease), microbiologists routinely exposed to N. meningitidis isolates, or anyone identified by public health officials as at increased risk during a serogroup B outbreak. Unlike the MenACWY risk-group list, HIV infection is notably NOT listed as an independent indication for MenB vaccination.

supplementalTopics.title: Booster Dosing for Ongoing Risk
supplementalTopics.summary: People 10 or older with an ongoing risk factor (complement deficiency, complement inhibitor use, asplenia, or routine occupational exposure) should get a MenB booster dose 1 year after completing the primary series, then every 2-3 years for as long as the risk persists. For someone vaccinated during a serogroup B outbreak specifically, a one-time booster is recommended if at least 1 year has passed since completing the primary series (public health officials may consider as short as a 6-month interval depending on the outbreak's trajectory).

keyPoints: Serogroup B causes about 60% of invasive meningococcal disease in people under 24 in the US, but routine adolescent MenACWY vaccination does not protect against it at all
Trumenba and Bexsero are not interchangeable - switching brands mid-series means starting a fresh series with the new brand plus at least a 4-week gap from the last dose of the old brand

The recommended dosing schedule differs by indication: a 3-dose Trumenba series for high-risk individuals versus a 2-dose Trumenba series (different interval) for healthy 16-23 year olds under shared clinical decision-making
College students face more than 3 times the serogroup B risk of similarly aged non-students, and university outbreaks have been a recurring US surveillance finding
Composite bactericidal response rates in trials ranged as low as 63%-66% depending on the study and timepoint, notably lower than typical MenACWY response rates
HIV infection is a MenACWY risk indication but is NOT listed as an independent indication for MenB vaccination
